scope: Child nutrition screening and caregiver education support for children from birth through 59 completed months (target platform scope: 0 to 72 completed months; 60 to 72 months screening rules planned for Phase 2). It does not diagnose malnutrition, nutrient deficiency, disease, or medical conditions, and is not a prescription or emergency service.

age_bands.label: Birth to 5 months
age_bands.variety_target: Exclusive milk only (0 complementary food groups). Breast milk or clinician-guided infant formula meets all hydration and nutritional needs.
age_bands.meal_cadence: On-demand feeding (typically 8–12 feeds in 24 hours for newborns, following hunger and fullness cues).

examples: Mother's breast milk or screened donor milk
food_categories.key_nutrients: Optimal balance of proteins, fats, lactose, antibodies, and micronutrients

examples: Clinician-prescribed or standard iron-fortified infant formula (when breastfeeding is not possible or sufficient)
food_categories.key_nutrients: Balanced macronutrients and iron for formula-fed infants

age_bands.safe_textures: Liquid milk only. Infant swallowing reflex is not yet equipped for solids.
foods_to_avoid: Water, sugar water, or herbal teas (risk of water intoxication, electrolyte imbalance, nutrient dilution)
Infant cereals, baby purees, or solid foods before 4–6 months
Cow's milk, goat's milk, or plant-based milks as a drink
Honey (infant botulism hazard)
core_guidance: Exclusive breastfeeding is recommended for the first 6 months when possible; this means breast milk only, including no water.
If breastfeeding is not possible or sufficient, feeding decisions and formula preparation should be guided by a qualified clinician and local public-health advice.
Do not begin complementary foods before 4 months.
age_bands.feeding_skills: Feeding is milk-based; assess feeding concerns with a qualified health professional.
safety: Seek urgent medical advice for poor feeding with lethargy, breathing difficulty, dehydration, or very few wet diapers.

age_bands.label: 6 to 8 months
age_bands.variety_target: Introduce 2 to 4 food groups gradually alongside continued frequent breast milk or formula. Focus on iron-rich staples and single-ingredient exposures.
age_bands.meal_cadence: Offer 2 to 3 small complementary meals daily + on-demand breast milk or formula.

examples: Pureed beef, chicken, turkey
Iron-fortified infant cereals (oat, barley)
Pureed lentils, split peas, or white beans
food_categories.key_nutrients: Iron, zinc, protein (critical as fetal iron stores deplete around 6 months)

examples: Mashed or pureed cooked sweet potato
Cooked carrots
Pureed squash
Steamed pureed zucchini or green beans
food_categories.key_nutrients: Vitamin A, beta-carotene, dietary fiber, minerals

examples: Mashed ripe avocado
Mashed ripe banana
Steamed unsweetened applesauce
Pureed ripe pear or peach
food_categories.key_nutrients: Vitamin C, potassium, healthy fatty acids

examples: Smooth peanut butter thinned with warm water or breast milk
Well-cooked scrambled or pureed whole egg
food_categories.key_nutrients: Protein, choline; early safe introduction reduces future allergy risk

age_bands.safe_textures: Smooth purees progressing toward thicker mashes with soft, small tender lumps as oral motor control develops.
foods_to_avoid: Honey (strict botulism hazard before 12 months)
Cow's milk or fortified plant milks as a drink before 12 months
Raw or undercooked eggs, meats, or seafood
Added salt, sugar, honey, or artificial sweeteners
Hard, round foods that pose choking hazards (whole grapes, raw apple wedges, whole nuts)
core_guidance: Begin safe, nutritionally adequate complementary foods around 6 months while continuing breastfeeding where applicable.
Start with small amounts; offer 2 to 3 meals daily, increasing texture and variety gradually.
Prioritize iron-rich foods and a variety of food groups; responsive feeding means noticing hunger and fullness cues.
age_bands.feeding_skills: When developmentally ready, offer smooth mashed or pureed foods, progressing toward thicker textures. Sit the child upright and supervise every meal.
safety: Do not give cow's milk or fortified dairy alternatives as a drink before 12 months.
Introduce allergenic foods alongside other foods; severe eczema or egg allergy requires clinician guidance before peanut introduction.

age_bands.label: 9 to 11 months
age_bands.variety_target: Aim for 3 to 5 diverse food groups daily. Promote oral chewing skills and independent grasp with appropriately sized finger foods.
age_bands.meal_cadence: Offer 3 to 4 meals daily + 1 to 2 nutritious snacks + continued milk feeds.

examples: Shredded tender chicken or soft flaked fish (carefully deboned)
Soft scrambled egg pieces
Soft tofu cubes
Cooked black beans, chickpeas, or lentils gently mashed
food_categories.key_nutrients: High-quality protein, zinc, iron, omega-3 fatty acids

examples: Soft cooked pasta shapes (spirals, shells)
Whole grain toast fingers
Soft cooked brown rice, oatmeal, or barley porridge
Steamed potato wedges
food_categories.key_nutrients: Complex carbohydrates, B vitamins, energy density

examples: Soft steamed carrot or broccoli florets
Ripe banana cut into bite pieces
Soft avocado cubes
Ripe strawberries or blueberries cut into quarters
food_categories.key_nutrients: Vitamin A, vitamin C, antioxidants, dietary fiber

examples: Pasteurized plain whole-milk yogurt
Pasteurized mild cheese strips or shredded cheddar
food_categories.key_nutrients: Calcium, fat, fat-soluble vitamins (as food ingredients, not liquid drink)

age_bands.safe_textures: Minced, chopped, or soft finger foods the child can grasp with fingertips. Soft enough to easily squish between thumb and forefinger.
foods_to_avoid: Whole round grapes, large berries, or cherry tomatoes (must be quartered lengthwise)
Whole nuts, whole seeds, popcorn, or hard chips
Raw hard carrots or apples (must be cooked until soft or finely grated)
Thick blobs or spoonfuls of peanut butter (must be spread thinly)
Honey (<12 months) and added sugars
core_guidance: Continue varied, nutrient-dense complementary foods and breastfeeding where applicable.
Offer 3 to 4 meals daily; 1 to 2 nutritious snacks can be added as needed.
Make textures progressively thicker and more varied as chewing and self-feeding skills develop.
age_bands.feeding_skills: Many infants can manage appropriately prepared finger foods from about 8 months; tailor texture and pieces to the individual child's ability.
safety: Cut, cook, mash, or thinly spread foods to reduce choking risk; avoid hard, sticky, round, or small foods.
Stay with the child and keep them seated upright while eating.

age_bands.label: 12 to 23 months
age_bands.variety_target: UNICEF Minimum Dietary Diversity Indicator: At least 5 of 8 food groups daily (breast milk, grains/roots, pulses/nuts, dairy, flesh foods, eggs, vitamin-A fruits/veg, other fruits/veg).
age_bands.meal_cadence: Offer 3 to 4 family meals daily + 1 to 2 wholesome snacks as needed.

examples: Continued breastfeeding up to 2 years or beyond
Pasteurized whole cow's milk (up to 16–24 oz/day)
Plain whole-milk yogurt
Cottage cheese
food_categories.key_nutrients: Calcium, healthy fats, vitamin D, immune factors

examples: Oatmeal, brown rice, whole wheat bread/roti, quinoa
Mashed or roasted sweet potatoes, potatoes, yams
Lentils (dal), hummus, cooked chickpeas, black beans
Smooth peanut or almond butter thinly spread on bread
food_categories.key_nutrients: Plant protein, zinc, iron, healthy monounsaturated fats

examples: Tender chicken, turkey, beef, lamb, salmon, cod (boneless)
Whole eggs (scrambled, hard-boiled and chopped)
food_categories.key_nutrients: Heme iron (highly absorbable), complete proteins, choline, B12

examples: Cooked spinach, kale, carrots, pumpkin, cantaloupe, ripe mango
Bananas, apples, pears, green peas, steamed zucchini, cucumbers
food_categories.key_nutrients: Immune support, eyesight protection, vitamin C, diverse gut microbiota

age_bands.safe_textures: Family table foods adapted for chewing and biting. Cut hot dogs and round grapes lengthwise into quarters. Supervise meals.
foods_to_avoid: Added sugars (candy, cookies, sugary breakfast cereals, chocolate)
Sugar-sweetened beverages (fruit juices, soda, flavored milk, sweetened teas)
Unpasteurized juices, milks, or cheeses; raw or undercooked animal products
Excessive salt in cooking
Large choking hazards: whole nuts, sticky marshmallows, hard candies, tough meats
core_guidance: Continue breastfeeding up to 2 years or beyond if desired, alongside family foods adapted for safety and texture.
Offer 3 to 4 meals daily and 1 to 2 nutritious snacks as needed.
Aim for dietary diversity: UNICEF's 6–23 month indicator uses foods from at least 5 of 8 groups in the preceding day.
age_bands.feeding_skills: Most children can eat family foods with safe preparation; encourage self-feeding without force.
safety: Keep added sugars out of infants' and young children's diets.
Avoid raw or undercooked eggs, meat, seafood, unpasteurized dairy/juice, and unwashed produce.

age_bands.label: 2 to 5 years
age_bands.variety_target: Diverse family plate targeting all main food groups across color spectrums: half vegetables and whole fruits, quarter whole grains, quarter lean protein foods, accompanied by water and pasteurized dairy.
age_bands.meal_cadence: 3 structured meals + 2 planned healthy snacks daily at consistent times.

examples: Colorful rainbow: bell peppers, broccoli, tomatoes, carrots, berries, melons, apples, oranges
food_categories.key_nutrients: Fiber, phytonutrients, vitamin C, potassium, immune resilience

examples: Whole wheat pasta, brown rice, whole grain bread, rolled oats, corn, millet
food_categories.key_nutrients: Slow-release energy, gut health fibers, magnesium

examples: Lentils, beans, tofu, eggs, poultry, fish, lean meats, finely chopped nuts or nut butters
food_categories.key_nutrients: Muscle development, enzymatic growth, bioavailable iron and zinc

examples: Pasteurized whole or low-fat cow's milk (or fortified soy milk)
Plain yogurt
Abundant plain water (primary beverage)
food_categories.key_nutrients: Bone-building calcium and vitamin D; optimal cellular hydration

age_bands.safe_textures: Family meals; continue to cut round or firm items (cherry tomatoes, sausages, grapes). Model safe eating habits.
foods_to_avoid: Sugary drinks, fruit punch, sodas, energy drinks, and flavored milk
Ultra-processed convenience snacks high in sodium and saturated/trans fats
Caffeinated beverages
Unpasteurized dairy, raw sprouts, or undercooked meats
Choking hazards without active supervision (hard candies, whole large nuts)
core_guidance: Build regular meals and nutritious snacks around a variety of minimally processed foods: vegetables and fruits, legumes, grains, protein foods, and dairy or appropriate alternatives.
Use responsive feeding: caregivers decide what is offered; the child decides whether and how much to eat from the offered foods.
Use WHO growth standards from birth to 5 years with a qualified health professional to interpret growth over time.
age_bands.feeding_skills: Maintain calm, seated meals and model varied foods; avoid pressure or restrictive diets unless a clinician directs them.
safety: Choking risk persists—prepare foods for the child’s chewing ability and supervise.
Choose pasteurized foods and safe food handling practices.

red_flags: difficulty breathing, blue color, or an active choking episode
signs of dehydration, lethargy, or persistent vomiting
poor growth, weight loss, feeding pain, swallowing difficulty, or a suspected food allergy reaction
prematurity, low birth weight, chronic disease, metabolic condition, or a prescribed therapeutic diet
